title: Template lens versus J-lens on single-token intermediates
takeaway: Re-running the appendix's readout and swap evaluations on the paper's original 50-item multi-hop benchmark, where every unspoken intermediate is a single token, leaves the two lenses at rough parity: the template lens reads out slightly more intermediates (84% against 76%) and redirects slightly fewer answers (52% against 68%). Both gaps sit inside overlapping 95% Wilson intervals, so the figure supports only the claim that the template lens buys nothing here, not that either lens is better.
walkthrough:
The item is a pair of bar panels the article draws live. Each panel carries two bars, one per lens, with a vertical whisker for the confidence interval. The widget prints `n = 50` beneath them, and hovering a bar reveals its raw count.

The 50 items are the [[multihop-benchmark]]: two-hop factual questions whose surface words have no direct association with the answer. "The color of the planet fourth from the Sun is" requires computing Mars before red can be produced. The same 50 prompts carry the [[internal-reasoning]] swap experiment in the body of the paper, run by default on [[claude-model-family|Sonnet 4.5]]. Every one of the 50 unspoken intermediates is a single vocabulary token.

That last property is the reason this figure exists. The [[template-lens]] was built to get past the [[single-token-limitation]] of the [[jacobian-lens]], and the preceding figure showed it holding up on two-, three- and four-token intermediates where the J-lens collapses. That comparison used a different distribution of prompts. This figure re-runs the identical readout and swap evaluations on the paper's original benchmark, where the J-lens faces no handicap at all.

The left panel, "Decoding the intermediate concept", asks how often each lens places the unspoken intermediate among its top ten tokens. The J-lens manages 38 of 50, or 76 percent. The template lens manages 42 of 50, or 84 percent.

The right panel, "Swapping the intermediate concept", is causal rather than correlational. It applies a [[lens-coordinate-swap]], exchanging the intermediate's coordinate for that of an alternative concept, and counts the prompts whose answer follows the swapped-in concept. The axis label notes $\alpha = 1$, the unit [[swap-strength-alpha|swap strength]]: the source vector is subtracted once and the target added once, with no doubling. The J-lens manages 34 of 50, or 68 percent. The template lens manages 26 of 50, or 52 percent.

The paper reads this as parity, with the template lens modestly overperforming on readouts and underperforming on swaps. The error bars are [[wilson-interval|95 percent Wilson intervals]], and they overlap heavily in both panels. At 50 items neither gap is resolved.

The conclusion the appendix draws is a narrow one. On single-token concepts the template lens is roughly at par with the J-lens, and its advantage in the previous figure is confined to intermediates the J-lens cannot name.

terms.definition: The title of the left panel. It scores each lens as a read-only tool: how often the lens surfaces the concept the model must infer but never says.
The left panel's y-axis. For each prompt the lens produces a ranked list over its vocabulary, and the item counts as a success when the known intermediate appears in the first ten entries.
The title of the right panel. It scores each lens as an intervention tool: whether writing a different concept into the lens coordinate redirects the model's answer.

terms.term: P(answer follows the swap) at α = 1
terms.definition: The right panel's y-axis. It is the fraction of prompts on which the top output token becomes the answer appropriate to the swapped-in concept rather than the original one, with the swap applied at unit strength.
The multiplier on the swap. At α = 1 the source concept's vector is subtracted once and the target's added once; elsewhere the paper also reports α = 2, which doubles both.

The first bar in each panel, and the first legend entry. It is the Jacobian lens applied to the first token of the intermediate word; on this benchmark every intermediate is one token long, so the first token is the whole word.

The second bar in each panel, and the second legend entry. The template for a word is the mean residual-stream activation over passages that end just before the word, centered against the mean over all other words and multiplied by the inverse covariance matrix; that whitening step is what the label names.
The concept a prompt requires the model to compute on the way to its answer, which appears neither in the prompt nor in the output. Mars, in the question about the color of the fourth planet.

The 50 two-hop factual prompts this figure runs on. Items were built so that the trigger word and the answer rarely co-occur without the bridging entity, which makes direct retrieval of the answer unlikely.
The whisker on each bar. It is a confidence interval for a proportion that stays inside [0, 1] and behaves sensibly at small counts, which matters at n = 50.
The line the widget prints under the two panels. It is the number of benchmark items behind every bar in the figure.
The middle band of layers where the paper finds the J-space acting as a workspace. The swap protocol inherited from the preceding figure applies the intervention across this full range.
The model the paper reports on by default, and so the model behind these bars. The appendix does not name a different one for this comparison.

The constraint the template lens was introduced to relieve: the J-lens has one vector per vocabulary token, so it cannot name a concept like blackmail or photosynthesis that spans several tokens. This benchmark is the case where the limitation does not bite.

numbers.meaning: Items in the benchmark, and the denominator of every bar. These are the same 50 two-hop factual prompts used for the internal-reasoning swap experiment in the body of the paper; the caption notes that all 50 latent intermediates are single tokens.
J-lens readout success: on 38 of the 50 prompts the intermediate concept appears in the lens's top ten. This is the left panel's first bar.
The 95% Wilson interval on the J-lens readout bar. Its width, about 23 points, is what 50 trials buys at a success rate near three quarters.

Template-lens readout success: 42 of 50 intermediates land in the top ten. This is the left panel's second bar, and the sense in which the text says the template lens modestly overperforms on readouts.
The 95% Wilson interval on the template-lens readout bar. It overlaps the J-lens interval across most of its length, so the 8-point readout gap is not resolved at this sample size.
J-lens swap success: on 34 of 50 prompts the swap moves the target-appropriate answer to the top of the output distribution. The right panel's first bar.
The 95% Wilson interval on the J-lens swap bar.
Template-lens swap success: 26 of 50. The right panel's second bar, and the sense in which the text says the template lens underperforms on swaps.
The 95% Wilson interval on the template-lens swap bar. It overlaps the J-lens swap interval, so the 16-point gap, though larger than the readout gap, is also not separated from zero here.
The cutoff for the readout metric: an intermediate counts as decoded when it ranks in the top ten of the lens's output over the vocabulary. A looser cutoff would raise both bars.
The swap strength used in the right panel. Unit strength means one subtraction of the source vector and one addition of the target; the paper reports α = 2 elsewhere when unit strength fails.
The coverage level of the Wilson intervals drawn as whiskers.
The J-lens swap success rate reported for Sonnet 4.5 on this same 50-item benchmark in the body of the paper. It sits close to the 68% here, though the two runs need not share every protocol detail.
The size of the word list for which templates were built. It bounds what the template lens can name at all, since its vocabulary must be enumerated in advance.
